adjudication_label: Nanoindentation depth and size effect in irradiated layers
canonical_question: Why is the indentation depth strictly limited to 200 nm when the irradiated layer is 200–300 nm deep, and how does this mitigate the 'size effect' mentioned?

question_variants.question: Why is the indentation depth strictly limited to 200 nm when the irradiated layer is 200–300 nm deep, and how does this mitigate the 'size effect' mentioned?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The text specifies the indentation depth was 200 nm and the irradiated layer is 200-300 nm deep, but it does not explicitly explain the rationale for the depth limit or how it mitigates the 'size effect'.

answers.answer: The paper states that hardness and modulus measurements were obtained at 200 nm indentation depth, but does not provide the specific rationale for why this depth was chosen to mitigate the size effect relative to the 200-300 nm irradiated layer.
answers.boundary_limitation: No explicit discussion of size effect mitigation strategy
evidence_spans: The results here demonstrate that grain refinement only occurred when the heavy ions are introduced.
This suggests that such a grain refinement observed in the dual-beam irradiation case was caused by a cascade effect.
The in situ nature of the experiments performed in this work has allowed us to observe the grain refinement effect in real-time
